title: Are 1156 and 2800 perfect squares? Do trailing zeros help?
description: One thousand one hundred fifty six and two thousand eight hundred are broken into primes and the primes are matched in pairs. Keeko doubts the second number, because it ends in two zeros.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number is a perfect square only when every prime in it has a partner. Watch for students who trust the zeros at the end and never look at the other primes.

source: Using prime factorisation, find whether 1156 and 2800 are pe
video_script.why: The child tests two numbers by pairing their primes, and sees that zeros at the end do not decide it.
video_script.substitution: Write the number as primes and look for a partner for each prime.
video_script.anchor: the two numbers of the book question, one thousand one hundred fifty six and two thousand eight hundred, on cards
video_script.wrong_answer: two thousand eight hundred is a perfect square
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees two zeros at the end of two thousand eight hundred and says it is a perfect square. The seven has no partner, so it is not.
video_script.payoff_line: One thousand one hundred fifty six is thirty four squared, a perfect square

final_answer.value: 1156 = 34² is a perfect square; 2800 is not
final_answer.spoken: one thousand one hundred fifty six is thirty four squared, a perfect square; two thousand eight hundred is not

maths_rules: 2800 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 7; the 7 appears once, so 2800 is not a perfect square
video_script.design: One idea: every prime needs a partner. Wrong idea: zeros at the end make a square. The two cards stay in the anchor band and the prime lines sit on the working board.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>It gives two numbers, one thousand one hundred fifty six and two thousand eight hundred.
<bookmark mark='use'/>The book asks us to use prime factorisation to decide.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each of them a perfect square?

beats.on_screen: the two cards hold still and the words perfect square? glow

marks.stop: the words perfect square? glow in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a row of coloured prime tiles; matching tiles join into pairs, and one tile is left without a match

marks.tiles: a row of prime tiles appears
marks.pairs: matching tiles join up in pairs

narration: <bookmark mark='tiles'/>A perfect square is a whole number multiplied by itself.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>Its primes can be matched in pairs, one from each copy.
<bookmark mark='left'/>If even one prime is left alone, the number is not a perfect square.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are one thousand one hundred fifty six and two thousand eight hundred.

beats.on_screen: To find: is each of 1156 and 2800 a perfect square?

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether each of them is a perfect square.

marks.pf1: the words prime factorisation of 1156 are written
marks.list1: 1156 = 2 × 2 × 17 × 17 is written, one prime at a time

narration: <bookmark mark='pf1'/>Step one, use prime factorisation on one thousand one hundred fifty six.
<bookmark mark='list1'/>It is two times two times seventeen times seventeen.

beats.on_screen: 1156 = (2 × 17) × (2 × 17): the four primes slide into two equal groups

marks.share: the four primes slide into two group boxes

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step two, match the primes into two equal groups.
<bookmark mark='each'/>Each group gets one two and one seventeen.

beats.on_screen: prime factorisation of 2800: 2800 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 7; the 2s and the 5s pair up, the 7 stays outside in the warning colour

marks.pf2: the words prime factorisation of 2800 are written
marks.alone: the 2s and the 5s join in pairs, and the 7 stays outside

narration: <bookmark mark='pf2'/>Step three, use prime factorisation on two thousand eight hundred.
<bookmark mark='list2'/>It is four twos, then two fives, then a seven.
<bookmark mark='alone'/>The twos and the fives make pairs, but the seven has no partner.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 2 × 17 = 34, so 1156 = 34 × 34 = 34², a perfect square; 2800 is not a perfect square

marks.no: 2800 is marked not a perfect square

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each group is two times seventeen, which is thirty four.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>One thousand one hundred fifty six is thirty four squared, a perfect square.
<bookmark mark='no'/>Two thousand eight hundred is not a perfect square.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says 2800 is a perfect square because of its two zeros; the zeros glow, then the lone 7 flashes and the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble appears and the two zeros at the end of 2800 glow
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks two thousand eight hundred is a perfect square, because it ends in two zeros.
<bookmark mark='alone'/>But look at the seven. It appears only once.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Zeros at the end do not pair up the other primes.
